lede:
Round 3 found that gradient-L1 improves accuracy but not sharpness. Round 4 tried the remaining lever: a small conditional PatchGAN term (LSGAN, spectral norm, as in Experiment 1). Each run starts from the round 3 gradient-L1 multi-date model (r3_g05_s0) and fine-tunes for 2,000 steps at weight 0.001, 0.003 or 0.01. The control runs the same fine-tune at weight 0, so extra training is not mistaken for a GAN effect. The GPU belonged to Experiment 5. Round 4 waited under the shared lock until no Experiment 5 training process was running, then trained one job at a time at batch 16. All scoring ran on CPU.

In short: at weight 0.01 the adversarial term makes the output a little sharper and removes much of the input-grid imprint. But the added detail is less correlated with the truth, and missed edges increase, especially on near-holdout tiles. X-band edge placement does not move. The term adds texture, not structure, so we do not adopt it.
choice:
Choice on validation

The rule, fixed before any run: compared with the control on validation (multi-date target), a weight is eligible only if MAE rises by at most 0.01 dB, invented-edge chamfer by at most 0.6 m and grid imprint by at most 0.05 (round 3 seed noise). It wins if it also gains sharpness: fine-detail energy up by more than 0.004, or missed-edge chamfer down by more than 0.6 m. Weights 0.001 and 0.003 changed almost nothing (all differences within noise). Weight 0.01 won on fine-detail energy (+0.024) and also cut the grid imprint by 0.32. Two warning signs sat outside the rule: missed edges rose by 1.0 m and detail correlation fell from 0.30 to 0.28.
hold:
Holdouts, two seeds each

Against the multi-date target, both GAN seeds behave the same way, and so do both control seeds:

  • Sharper, less gridded: fine-detail energy 0.407 to 0.418 vs 0.394 to 0.395 (far) and 0.353 to 0.368 vs 0.329 (near). Grid imprint falls to 1.83 to 1.94 from 2.10 (far) and to 1.86 to 2.03 from 3.08 (near).
  • Less faithful: detail correlation drops (far 0.332 to 0.338 vs 0.345 to 0.346; near 0.273 to 0.278 vs 0.293), SSIM drops, and MAE rises by about 0.01 dB. Missed edges rise slightly on far tiles (+0.2 to 0.3 m) and sharply on near tiles (36.6 to 38.6 m vs 32.8 to 33.1 m), though invented edges fall there.
  • Against the single-date target the pattern is the same, more starkly on near tiles: detail correlation 0.084 to 0.089 vs 0.120, and missed edges 37.6 to 40.4 m vs 30.9 to 31.1 m.

Rising detail energy together with falling detail correlation means the new detail does not land where the true detail is. The panels agree: the GAN adds a fine grain over the control's smooth fields. It does not recover the street grid or building rows that the 40 MHz truth shows.
xband:
Hallucination check against X-band

We scored the control and the GAN with the same X-band edge check as round 2: held-out Umbra and ICEYE sites in the near and far holdout frames, plus the X-band test and tuning sites inside training frames (Capella, Umbra and ICEYE). Chamfer is measured on infrastructure pixels only. The GAN neither gains nor loses against X-band geometry. Every difference from the control is under 1 m: invented edges (p2x) differ by at most 0.3 m, and missed edges (x2p) by at most 0.8 m, with Capella test sites 31.8 vs 32.6 m and far Umbra 22.8 vs 22.9 m. The added texture is fine enough that it neither creates nor removes edges at the X-band scale. That is consistent with texture rather than invented structures. The X-band panels show the GAN output nearly identical to the control at the site scale.
caveats:
• One adversarial design (conditional PatchGAN, LSGAN, 2,000 fine-tune steps); a perceptual loss or a longer GAN schedule could behave differently.
  • Two seeds each for the winner and the control. The seed spread is small (≤0.006 in detail correlation, ≤2 m in near missed edges), well below the GAN-vs-control gaps reported above.
  • The selection rule did not include detail correlation, so the validation winner was allowed to lower it; the holdouts then confirmed that drop.
  • Incident: while stopping our first round 4 attempt (which ran beside Experiment 5 and slowed it), an over-broad process filter also killed two Experiment 5 runs. Experiment 5's queue restarted both from scratch within the minute. Our filter now matches only Experiment 3's training script, and Round 4 then waited for Experiment 5 to finish.
